lines: Week two: text classification. A function takes a text and returns one label from a fixed set.
Spam or ham is binary. Sports, politics or tech is multi-class. Sentiment is the classic example.
Every project follows the same loop: data, then features, then a model, then predictions, then evaluation, and back to the data.
Method one: Naive Bayes. It asks which class is most likely to have produced these words.
It multiplies the class prior by the probability of each word given the class.
Naive means it assumes the words are independent once the class is known. Not good is just not, plus good.
If a word never appeared with a class, its probability is zero, and the whole product becomes zero. Add-one smoothing fixes that.
It is generative, fast, and works with very little data. That makes it the baseline.
Method two: logistic regression. Despite the name, it is a classifier.
It adds up weighted features into one score z, then a sigmoid squeezes z into a probability between zero and one.
Positive weights push toward the positive class, negative weights push away. Above zero point five, predict positive.
It is discriminative: it learns the boundary directly. Its weights are easy to read, but the boundary is a straight line.
Method three: the support vector machine.
Many lines can separate two classes. The SVM picks the one with the widest margin to the nearest points.
Those nearest points are the support vectors. A kernel lets it bend the boundary when the data is not linear.
It is strong in high dimensions, but slow on very large data, and its score is not a probability.
The model only sees the features you give it.
Statistical features: length, exclamation marks, capital letters. Lexical features: bag of words, TF-IDF, n-grams.
Linguistic features: parts of speech and sentiment lexicons. Domain features: spam words or emoticons.
The project plan: start with Naive Bayes as a baseline, then logistic regression, then an SVM if time allows.
